deep.reconstruction: This page contains no mathematics. It is part of the historical preface (the 'Summarium') in Novi Commentarii Tom. X, which introduces Euler's E296 'Elementa calculi variationum' and E297 'Analytica explicatio methodi maximorum et minimorum'. The previous page noted that the ancients knew the circle encloses the greatest area for a given perimeter but never attacked the question directly. This page continues the story in three steps. (1) Johann Bernoulli posed and solved the brachistochrone problem (1696–97): among all curves joining a higher point to a lower one, find the one along which a heavy body descends in the shortest time. He found the answer is the cycloid. (2) Johann's method gave his older brother Jacob the occasion to consider the 'great isoperimetric problem'. In its broadest form this asks: among all curves between two given points that share a common property (equal length, hence the name 'isoperimetric', or some other common property), find the one that encloses maximal area, generates maximal solid of revolution about a given axis, or in general has some maximum or minimum property. In modern terms this is a variational problem with an integral constraint, which the Lagrange-multiplier rule later handles. (3) The writer weighs Jacob's method: one cannot tell whether to admire more his patience in long, tedious calculations or his sagacity in drawing elegant conclusions. Because the conclusions were elegant, one suspected a shorter route existed. Johann took that route; it at first failed in some 'too hidden' cases (his 1697/1706 errors), but he later made up for this generously after a deeper re-treatment (1718). The next page continues with Euler's own work (Methodus inveniendi, 1744) and the motivation for the new analytic 'method of variations' in E296.
errors: Minor historical simplification. Johann Bernoulli's published brachistochrone solution used an optical analogy (Fermat's principle, refraction through layered media), not a general method. It was Jacob's own brachistochrone solution, varying two adjacent ordinates, that foreshadowed the isoperimetric technique. Jacob issued the isoperimetric challenge in 1697 partly as a counter-challenge to his brother, not merely as an extension of Johann's method. The page's statement that Johann's method 'gave occasion' to Jacob is a defensible but loose reading.
